did_you_know.text: Did you know? After King Ahasuerus’s anger toward Vashti subsided, he remembered her and the decree issued against her. Thus began the search for a new queen.

Did you know? Mordecai is described as a Jewish man living in Susa the citadel. His ancestry was linked to a family of exiles from Jerusalem who had been deported during the reign of Jeconiah, king of Judah.
Did you know? Esther was also called Hadassah. She had lost both her father and mother, and Mordecai, her cousin, had taken her as his own daughter.
Did you know? Mordecai had instructed Esther not to reveal her people or her nationality, so her Jewish identity remained a secret when she first entered the palace.

Did you know? Mordecai did more than simply give Esther instructions; every day he walked back and forth in front of the courtyard of the women’s quarters to learn how she was doing and what would happen to her.
Did you know? The young women brought to the king underwent a twelve-month preparation period: six months with myrrh oil and six months with perfumes and women’s cosmetics.

Did you know? According to the text, the young woman went to the king in the evening and returned in the morning to the second women’s quarters. She did not go to him again unless the king was pleased with her and called for her by name.
Did you know? When it was Esther’s turn, she asked for nothing beyond what Hegai, the keeper of the women, suggested. Even so, she won the favor of everyone who saw her.
Did you know? Ahasuerus loved Esther more than all the other women, placed a royal crown on her head, and made her queen in place of Vashti.

Did you know? Mordecai uncovered the plot of Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king’s doorkeepers, and Esther reported it to Ahasuerus in Mordecai’s name. After the matter was investigated, the conspirators were hanged, and the event was recorded in the book of the royal annals in the king’s presence.
